Incus config template read/write primitive abuse (CVE-2026-48752) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation primitive for the Incus templates/ symlink escape: use of `incus config template create|edit|show` against an instance/image, which — when the image contained a top-level `templates` symlink — reads or writes arbitrary host files as root. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CLI verb chain the PoC uses to trigger host file access. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact PoC verbs (`incus config template create|edit|show`) that are the only interface through which the symlinked host directory is read/written; template use is uncommon enough for a hunt. Cross-checked GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479, DailyCVE and Eventus Security write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479 • https://dailycve.com/incus-arbitrary-file-read-write-via-unsanitized-symlink-cve-2026-48752-critical-dc-jun2026-681/ • https://advisory.eventussecurity.com/advisory/incus-vulnerabilities-break-host-instance-boundary/
ATT&CKT1611 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admins authoring cloud-init/config templates on instances via `incus config template edit`
  • CI/provisioning tooling (Packer-style) that ships images carrying templates and edits them post-import
  • Operator running `incus config template show` to audit an existing template
  • Incus documentation/lab walkthroughs exercising the template feature
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line and the account; confirm whether the target instance/image was imported from an untrusted tar shortly beforehand and whether the referenced template FILENAME resolves to a host path (e.g. an absolute /etc path) rather than an in-container relative path. 2) Contain: freeze/stop the instance, quarantine the imported image/backup tar, and revoke the user's `incus` group membership pending review. 3) Hunt: check `/etc/cron.d`, `/root/.ssh`, `/etc/sudoers.d`, `/etc/ld.so.preload` for recent writes by incusd, and inventory Incus version — anything < 6.0.6 / 6.21.0 is vulnerable.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "incus"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "config" and ProcessCommandLine has "template"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("create","edit","show")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incus"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "config" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "template"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("create","edit","show")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

incusd daemon writing to sensitive host paths (Incus templates symlink escape) AIInstallation High
Detects the Incus daemon (incusd, running as root) writing files into privileged host directories that live outside any container storage pool — the concrete host-filesystem escape produced by the templates/ symlink in a malicious image or backup. Article-specific because incusd has no legitimate reason to write /etc/cron.d, /root/.ssh, /etc/shadow, etc. Rationale: incusd is a root daemon whose legitimate writes stay inside the storage pool (e.g. /var/lib/incus); any write it makes to /etc/cron.d, /root/.ssh or /etc/shadow is the direct fingerprint of the symlink escape and the PoC's /etc/cron.d cronjob drop. Datadog left empty — the standard linux.auditd Datadog schema exposes no file-path attribute to pivot on. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479 • https://advisory.eventussecurity.com/advisory/incus-vulnerabilities-break-host-instance-boundary/ • https://dailycve.com/incus-arbitrary-file-read-write-via-unsanitized-symlink-cve-2026-48752-critical-dc-jun2026-681/
ATT&CKT1611 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Incus host-managed automation that legitimately edits /etc via a custom hook (rare, environment-specific)
  • Storage pool misconfigured to sit under /etc (highly unusual — verify pool path)
  • Backup/restore of a legitimately templated instance whose template path was misconfigured
  • Configuration-management tooling co-located on the host that shares the incusd binary name (verify full path /usr/sbin/incusd)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the written file and its contents — a cron entry running as root, an authorized_keys line, or a /etc/ld.so.preload path is confirmation of exploitation, not a benign write. 2) Contain: remove the malicious file, stop incusd, isolate the host, and rotate any credentials/keys reachable from it; quarantine the source image/backup tar. 3) Hunt: pull the preceding `incus image import` / `incus import` and `incus config template` commands (see companion UC), enumerate all instances created from untrusted images, and confirm Incus is patched to 6.0.6 / 6.21.0+.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "incusd"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/crontab","/root/.ssh","/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/etc/sudoers","/etc/sudoers.d","/etc/ld.so.preload")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incusd"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/crontab","/root/.ssh","/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/etc/sudoers","/etc/sudoers.d","/etc/ld.so.preload")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Untrusted Incus image/backup import immediately followed by template write AIExploitation High
Correlates an `incus image import` or `incus import` (backup restore) with an `incus config template create|edit` on the same host+user within one hour — the full CVE-2026-48752 exploitation sequence where an attacker imports a tar carrying a templates/ symlink then writes through it to the host. Higher fidelity than either event alone. Rationale: The import (deploy malicious container) followed within minutes by a template write is the complete PoC chain from the advisory; correlating the two on host+user removes the benign-template-edit false positives that UC1 alone carries. Sigma/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty — this is a cross-event temporal correlation not expressible as a single-event rule. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479 • https://dailycve.com/incus-arbitrary-file-read-write-via-unsanitized-symlink-cve-2026-48752-critical-dc-jun2026-681/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated provisioning that imports an image then applies a cloud-init template in the same run
  • Operator restoring a backup and immediately editing its config template legitimately
  • Golden-image build pipeline on a dedicated Incus host that always imports+templates in sequence
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the imported tar's origin and whether it contains a top-level `templates` entry that is a symlink (tar -tv); inspect the template FILENAME argument for an absolute host path. 2) Contain: stop and quarantine the instance and the source tar, revoke the user's `incus` group access, and snapshot the host for forensics. 3) Hunt: run the incusd sensitive-path-write UC to confirm host-side impact, review all images/backups imported by the same user, and verify/patch the Incus version to 6.0.6 / 6.21.0+.

    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)

    | where (ProcessCommandLine has "image" and ProcessCommandLine has "import") or (ProcessCommandLine has "import" and ProcessCommandLine has ".tar")
    | project ImportTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ImportCmd = ProcessCommandLine;

Incus lowlevel hook RCE — incusd spawns root shell at container start (CVE-2026-48751) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the payload half of the Incus restricted-project bypass: when a snapshot carrying a malicious raw.lxc/raw.qemu lowlevel hook is restored and the instance is started, the incusd container-monitor executes the attacker's lxc.hook.pre-start command as root on the host. This surfaces incusd/forkstart spawning a shell or discovery binary as root — the moment arbitrary command execution lands on the Incus server. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exploit mechanic: liblxc executes the raw.lxc `lxc.hook.pre-start` command as root under the incusd monitor (forkstart) at container start. Filtering forkstart/lxc-monitor parentage while excluding forkexec removes legit `incus exec` root shells, isolating the hook-fired RCE. Corroborated against the GHSA advisory (CVSS 9.9, fixed 7.2.0). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-48q5-w887-33wv • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-48q5-w887-33wv • https://dailycve.com/incus-restriction-bypass-via-snapshot-lowlevel-hook-injection-cve-2026-23953-high-dc-jun2026-680/
ATT&CKT1611 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmins in unrestricted/trusted projects legitimately using raw.lxc lxc.hook.pre-start for custom bind-mounts or GPU passthrough
  • Container entrypoint/init scripts that shell out and are attributed to the incusd/forkstart ancestry
  • Backup or monitoring tooling that registers a pre-start hook to quiesce services before snapshot
  • Interactive `incus exec <ctn> sh` as root (excluded by the forkexec filter, but variant tooling may re-introduce it)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "forkexec")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the child ProcessCommandLine — confirm the container name and whether the instance was recently received via `incus move --mode push` or `incus snapshot restore` into a project carrying restricted.containers.lowlevel=block. A root shell writing to unusual host paths (e.g. filesystem root) is high-signal. 2) Contain: `incus stop --force <instance>`, freeze the project, and snapshot the host for forensics; block further `incus move` transfers into restricted projects until patched. 3) Hunt: inspect the instance backup.yaml/config for raw.lxc or raw.qemu hook directives, review who holds can_edit on that instance, and confirm incusd is upgraded to >=7.2.0 (or 6.0.6/6.21.0) fleet-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "incusd"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("forkstart","[lxc monitor]") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "forkexec"   // pre-start hook context, exclude interactive `incus exec`
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","curl","wget","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "incusd" or ParentProcessName has "incusd"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("forkstart","lxc monitor") and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "forkexec"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/id","/curl","/wget","/python3","/perl","/nc","/ncat")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("root","")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious Incus raw.lxc / raw.qemu lowlevel hook injection via `incus config set` AIWeaponization Medium
Fleet-wide hunt for the weaponization step of CVE-2026-48751: an operator setting a raw.lxc or raw.qemu value that embeds a container lifecycle hook (lxc.hook.pre-start, lxc.init.cmd, lxc.execute.cmd) pointing at a shell command. This is the primitive an attacker crafts in an unrestricted project before snapshotting and moving the instance into a restricted project for root RCE. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC string shape — `incus config set ... raw.lxc='lxc.hook.pre-start = /bin/sh -c ...'` — combining the lowlevel key (raw.lxc/raw.qemu) with a lifecycle-hook directive. Legitimate raw.lxc use rarely pairs with an executable pre-start hook, making the combination high-fidelity. Hook directive names confirmed from the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lxc/incus/security/advisories/GHSA-48q5-w887-33wv • https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/reference/instance_options/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Advanced admins in unrestricted projects legitimately using raw.lxc lxc.hook.pre-start for bind-mounts, cgroup tweaks, or device passthrough
  • IaC/automation (Ansible, Terraform incus provider) templating raw.lxc/raw.qemu blocks that contain hooks
  • Lab/testing hosts where the CVE PoC or documentation examples are reproduced by staff
  • raw.qemu tuning that includes -cmdline style args without malicious intent
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full command line — decode the hook payload after `lxc.hook.*=` and confirm whether it invokes a shell/interpreter (`/bin/sh -c`, base64, curl) versus a benign mount helper. Identify the instance and project. 2) Contain: if the instance was subsequently moved (`incus move --mode push`) or snapshot-restored into a restricted project, treat the target host as potentially root-compromised — stop the instance and isolate. Revoke can_edit for the acting principal. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 on the destination host for incusd spawning a root shell; scan all instance backup.yaml files for raw.lxc/raw.qemu hooks and verify incusd version >=7.2.0 (or 6.0.6/6.21.0).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "incus"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "config" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("raw.lxc","raw.qemu")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("lxc.hook","hook.pre-start","hook.start","lxc.init.cmd","lxc.execute.cmd")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "incus"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("raw.lxc","raw.qemu")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("lxc.hook","hook.pre-start","lxc.init.cmd","lxc.execute.cmd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Lemur web worker fetching EC2 IMDS credentials path (acme_url SSRF to 169.254.169.254) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-55166: Lemur: ACME SSRF + creator-equality IDOR lead

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Lemur ACME worker-role STS credentials used from outside AWS (IMDS SSRF exfiltration, CVE-2026-55166) · [LLM] Anomalous private-key export from Lemur certificate key endpoint (creator-equality IDOR, CVE-2026-55166) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Lemur ACME worker-role STS credentials used from outside AWS (IMDS SSRF exfiltration, CVE-2026-55166) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the payoff of the acme_url SSRF: temporary EC2 instance-role credentials belonging to the Lemur worker (e.g. 'lemur-acme-role') being replayed by AWS API calls from a source IP outside the AWS/VPC range. This is the highest-fidelity signal that IMDS credentials were stolen via the Lemur authority-creation SSRF and are now being used off-instance. Rationale: Keys on the article's concrete role name 'lemur-acme-role' (matched loosely as *lemur* so it survives per-deployment naming) + AssumedRole type + a source IP outside AWS/RFC1918 — the exact shape GuardDuty labels InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS. Cross-checked AWS GuardDuty docs, MITRE T1552.005, and Datadog Security Labs' IMDS-theft write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v2wp-frmc-5q3v • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/ • https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-guardduty-enhances-detection-of-ec2-instance-credential-exfiltration/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/cloud-security-atlas/attacks/stealing-ec2-instance-role-credentials/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate NAT/egress IP that legitimately proxies EC2 role calls when workloads run behind an on-prem gateway
  • Third-party SaaS/monitoring vendor assuming the role cross-account from its own public IP range
  • CI/CD or IaC runner outside AWS legitimately using exported role credentials
  • Geo-IP/attribution error tagging an AWS-owned IP as external
  • VPN split-tunnel making an instance's calls appear to originate from a public IP
Suppression filter
and userIdentity.invokedBy not like /amazonaws.com/ and sourceIPAddress not like /^3\.|^13\.|^15\.|^18\.|^52\.|^54\./
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all CloudTrail events for the flagged AssumedRole session (accessKeyId + sessionIssuer) and confirm the source IP is genuinely non-AWS and the role is the Lemur instance profile; check GuardDuty for a matching InstanceCredentialExfiltration finding. 2) Contain: revoke the session via an inline Deny policy with an aws:TokenIssueTime condition (or detach/rotate the role), then force IMDSv2-only on the Lemur EC2 instance so GET-only SSRF can no longer read credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate every API action the stolen session performed (IAM changes, S3/KMS access, new access keys), review Lemur for rogue ACME authorities pointed at 169.254.169.254, and rotate any resources the role could touch.
title: Lemur Instance-Role Credentials Used From Outside AWS (CVE-2026-55166)
id: 6f1d2c8a-9b4e-4a71-8f2c-1a3e5d7c9b02
description: AssumedRole session tied to the Lemur ACME worker role makes AWS API calls from a non-AWS/non-RFC1918 source IP, indicating IMDS credential exfiltration via the acme_url SSRF.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v2wp-frmc-5q3v
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1552.005
  - attack.t1078.004
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    userIdentity.type: 'AssumedRole'
    userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName|contains: 'lemur'

Lemur web worker fetching EC2 IMDS credentials path (acme_url SSRF to 169.254.169.254) AIExploitation Low
Hunts the SSRF exploitation step itself: the Lemur application worker (python/gunicorn/celery) opening an HTTP connection to the link-local IMDS endpoint 169.254.169.254 as a result of the attacker-supplied acme_url. Any public-facing web worker reaching IMDS's security-credentials path is anomalous and, on IMDSv1, indicates credential theft in progress. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact IMDS target 169.254.169.254 combined with the Lemur worker process set — the on-wire trace of the acme_url SSRF. Low confidence because the AWS SDK (boto) legitimately hits the same IP for role-credential refresh; deploy scoped to the Lemur host(s) and treat as a hunt. IMDS-SSRF technique corroborated by Datadog Security Labs and MITRE T1552.005. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v2wp-frmc-5q3v • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/cloud-security-atlas/attacks/stealing-ec2-instance-role-credentials/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • boto3/botocore periodically refreshing instance-role credentials from IMDS (same IP, same python process) — the dominant benign source
  • AWS CLI or SSM agent on the host querying IMDS metadata
  • Container/EKS metadata proxy or a health-check probing 169.254.169.254
  • Config-management (Ansible/Chef) modules resolving instance identity via IMDS
  • Application code that legitimately reads region/AZ from IMDS on startup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("lemur","acme","authorit") or InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root","awssdk")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connecting process and whether the host is a Lemur worker; correlate the timestamp against inbound POSTs to /api/1/authorities and check whether the IMDS request targeted the iam/security-credentials path vs benign metadata. 2) Contain: enforce IMDSv2-only (HttpTokens=required, hop-limit=1) on the instance so GET-only SSRF cannot read credentials, and patch Lemur to 1.9.2. 3) Hunt: pivot to CloudTrail for off-instance use of the Lemur role (UC1), review Lemur for authorities whose acme_url is a link-local/RFC1918 address, and audit recently auto-provisioned SSO accounts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","gunicorn","uwsgi","celery","lemur","nginx")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254"
| summarize Conns=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by FirstSeen desc

Anomalous private-key export from Lemur certificate key endpoint (creator-equality IDOR, CVE-2026-55166) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the IDOR payoff: a single principal/IP pulling private keys from multiple certificates via GET /api/1/certificates/<id>/key. Because the creator branch always returns 200 even after ownership transfer, an attacker harvests PKI private keys; a burst of successful key exports by one caller is the article-specific web-log signature. Rationale: Anchors on Lemur's private-key export route /api/1/certificates/<id>/key (the sink at certificates/views.py:734) and a fan-out threshold (>=3 distinct keys per caller) to catch harvesting while suppressing single legitimate exports. Web-log-only detection since ownership context isn't in access logs; grounded in the advisory's IDOR description. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v2wp-frmc-5q3v • https://vulert.com/blog/critical-open-source-cves-security-roundup/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate PKI operator bulk-exporting keys during a CA migration or key-rotation project
  • Automation/service account that periodically exports keys for deployment pipelines
  • An admin troubleshooting several certificates and legitimately downloading their keys
  • Load-balancer/health-check hitting a certificate route (usually non-200 on /key, so filtered by status=200)
  • Backup tooling snapshotting certificate material
Suppression filter
| where SrcUsername !in~ ("pki-automation","cert-deploy-svc") and SrcUsername !endswith "-svc"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SrcUsername/SrcIp and whether it is a freshly auto-provisioned SSO account (cross-check Lemur user creation time and active=True), then list which certificates' keys were pulled and whether the caller is the current owner. 2) Contain: disable the offending Lemur account, revoke and reissue every certificate whose private key was exported (ownership transfer does NOT revoke creator access — the key must be rotated), and patch to Lemur 1.9.2. 3) Hunt: correlate the same principal to UC1 (stolen AWS role use) and UC2 (IMDS SSRF), and review authority-creation activity by the account.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)/api/1/certificates/[0-9]+/key"
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| summarize KeyExports=count(), DistinctKeys=dcount(Url), SampleUrls=make_set(Url, 25), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername
| where DistinctKeys >= 3   // one principal exporting >=3 distinct private keys in the window
| order by DistinctKeys desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_keys values(Web.uri_path) as uris min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.uri_path="/api/1/certificates/*/key" Web.status=200 by Web.src Web.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_keys >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - distinct_keys
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_keys values(Web.uri_path) as uris min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.uri_path="/api/1/certificates/*/key" Web.status=200 by Web.src Web.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_keys >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - distinct_keys
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] IIS web shell (w3wp.exe) spawning recon, curl exfil, or RAR staging · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CL-STA-1062 Targets Southeast Asian Governments and Critical Infrastructure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] TinyRCT backdoor masquerading as PerfWatson2.exe executing from %LOCALAPPDATA% · [LLM] Scheduled task persistence for GoogleUpdater or VMware-disguised VNT binary · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure · [LLM] SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Password-protected RAR staging of data for exfiltration (-hp) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
TinyRCT backdoor masquerading as PerfWatson2.exe executing from %LOCALAPPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 TinyRCT .NET backdoor, which masquerades as Visual Studio's PerfWatson2.exe but enforces an environment check that it runs only from %LOCALAPPDATA%. Legitimate PerfWatson2.exe ships inside the Visual Studio install tree under Program Files, so any PerfWatson2.exe launching from AppData\Local is article-specific TinyRCT behaviour. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade name PerfWatson2.exe plus TinyRCT's own self-imposed %LOCALAPPDATA% execution constraint; legitimate PerfWatson2 lives under Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio, making AppData\Local execution near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1497.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a portable/extracted copy of Visual Studio components from a profile folder
  • Visual Studio installer caching PerfWatson2 in AppData during an update (rare, usually Program Files)
  • Security tooling copying the binary to AppData for analysis on an analyst workstation
  • EDR sandbox detonation copying the sample into LocalAppData
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" and not(FolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and confirm it is not the signed Microsoft PerfWatson2 (legit is signed 'Microsoft Corporation' under Program Files). Check the parent process and whether the host concurrently beaconed to 45.32.113.172 or 139.180.134.221. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the AppData\Local copy; block both C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search the environment for any PerfWatson2.exe outside Program Files, for the GoogleUpdater scheduled task, and for choice.exe-based self-delete batch chains indicating TinyRCT cleanup.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PerfWatson2.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\PerfWatson2.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the two confirmed CL-STA-1062 IPs: 45.32.113.172 (TinyRCT HTTP C2, ~10s beacon) and 139.180.134.221 (payload/tool-staging server hosting the PerfWatson2.exe backdoor and RAR tool archives). Pure-IOC network detection for both beaconing and payload pull. Rationale: Both IPs are explicitly named in the article (139.180.134.221 hosting PerfWatson2.exe; 45.32.113.172 as TinyRCT C2 in the kill-chain block) and confirmed across the Unit 42 report and Talos UAT-7237 overlap; raw IOC hits are high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or sandbox sandboxing the sample and reaching the C2
  • Threat-intel scanning/validation services probing the IPs from a corporate range
  • Shared Vultr/cloud hosting reassigning the IP to a benign tenant after takedown (verify timestamps against report publication)
  • Internal vuln scanner configured to crawl flagged IOCs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process; if it is PerfWatson2.exe, a fake vmtools.exe, or curl.exe from a web-server context, treat as confirmed. Note beacon cadence (~10s = TinyRCT). 2) Contain: block both IPs at firewall/proxy, isolate the source host, and capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on src_ip for prior 139.180.134.221 downloads (RAR/SoftEther tool pulls), and sweep all hosts for second-stage payloads delivered from the staging server.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's habit of disguising tunneling tools (SoftEther VPN, VNT) as VMware system binaries such as vmtools.exe. Flags processes named vmtools/vmtoolsd whose signing company is not 'VMware, Inc.' or whose product string references SoftEther — i.e. a VMware-named binary that isn't VMware. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's Figure 6/7 masquerade (SoftEther disguised as vmtools.exe, VNT disguised as a VMware executable); the company-name/path mismatch separates the tunneler from genuine VMware Tools without needing a hash. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine VMware Tools where version metadata is stripped/empty after repackaging by an MSP
  • Older VMware Tools builds signed under a legacy company string ('VMware, Inc.' variations)
  • Third-party VM management tools legitimately named vmtools running from a non-standard path
  • Software-distribution systems staging VMware Tools in a temp folder before install
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\VMware\VMware Tools\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the binary's digital signature and the command line for SoftEther/VNT tunnel arguments (server address, listen port). Confirm it isn't VMware-signed. 2) Contain: terminate the tunneler, isolate the host, and block its configured remote VPN/relay endpoint. 3) Hunt: look for scheduled tasks launching the same disguised binary, RDP sessions riding the tunnel, and the same masquerade name on peer hosts indicating lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "VMware, Inc." or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "SoftEther"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ActingProcessFileCompany != "VMware, Inc." or ActingProcessFileProduct has "SoftEther"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessFileProduct, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task persistence for GoogleUpdater or VMware-disguised VNT binary AIInstallation Medium
Detects CL-STA-1062 establishing persistence via schtasks.exe creating a task named GoogleUpdater (TinyRCT loader) or a task launching a tunneler disguised as vmtools/VNT (Figure 7). Pivots on the task-creation command line rather than the binary itself. Rationale: Combines the article/kill-chain GoogleUpdater task name (TinyRCT loader) with the Figure 7 VNT-as-VMware scheduled task; task creation referencing these masquerade tokens is far more specific than generic schtasks alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Google Chrome/Updater creating GoogleUpdateTaskMachineCore tasks (note: name differs from 'GoogleUpdater')
  • VMware Tools installer registering a legitimate vmtools-related task
  • Admin scripts re-creating VMware service tasks during template provisioning
  • Software-packaging tools that template task names containing 'vmtools'
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\VMware\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (the binary path and arguments the task launches) and verify whether it points to a signed Google/VMware binary in its standard location. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task, isolate the host, and quarantine the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks across the fleet for the same name/binary, and correlate the task creator process — if it was a web shell (w3wp.exe) or PerfWatson2.exe, escalate to full IR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IIS web shell (w3wp.exe) spawning recon, curl exfil, or RAR staging AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 ASPX web-shell command-execution channel where the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd/curl/rar and native recon binaries — the actor piped system/network enumeration to actor IPs via curl and staged source code into RAR archives directly from the web shell. Rationale: Encodes the article's web-shell-as-execution-mechanism (Figure 4 curl enumeration, Figure 2 source-code archiving) via the w3wp.exe parent pivot — IIS workers should virtually never spawn curl, rar, tracert, or whoami. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web applications shelling out to net.exe/whoami for diagnostics
  • Application deployment scripts invoking cmd.exe under the app pool identity
  • Monitoring agents that run ipconfig/netstat from a web context
  • Developer health-check endpoints that exec systeminfo
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck", "\\Monitoring\\") and FileName in~ ("ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command lines — recon piped to curl targeting 45.32.113.172/139.180.134.221 or rar with -hp confirms malicious use; review IIS logs for the requesting URI and source IP (the web shell). 2) Contain: pull the offending .aspx file, isolate the web server, and reset the app-pool service account credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate recently written/modified .aspx files in web roots, and pivot on the source IP across other internet-facing servers for the same web-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe", "httpd.exe", "php-cgi.exe", "tomcat.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "curl.exe", "rar.exe", "whoami.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "tracert.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "netstat.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\curl.exe", @"\rar.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\ipconfig.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\tracert.exe", @"\systeminfo.exe", @"\netstat.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      - '\systeminfo.exe'
      - '\netstat.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:*\w3wp.exe OR @ParentImage:*\W3WP.exe) (@Image:*\cmd.exe OR @Image:*\curl.exe OR @Image:*\rar.exe OR @Image:*\whoami.exe OR @Image:*\ipconfig.exe OR @Image:*\net.exe OR @Image:*\tracert.exe OR @Image:*\systeminfo.exe OR @Image:*\netstat.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^w3wp\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|curl|rar|whoami|ipconfig|net|net1|tracert|systeminfo|netstat)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="w3wp.exe" Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","curl.exe","rar.exe","whoami.exe","ipconfig.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","tracert.exe","systeminfo.exe","netstat.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="w3wp.exe" Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","curl.exe","rar.exe","whoami.exe","ipconfig.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","tracert.exe","systeminfo.exe","netstat.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Password-protected RAR staging of data for exfiltration (-hp) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's data-staging step: compressing findings (MSSQL dumps, entire web-server source-code directories) into header-encrypted, password-protected RAR archives using the rar -hp flag prior to exfil. Pivots on the -hp<password> add-to-archive command line, which survives binary renaming. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit tradecraft of compressing findings into password-protected RAR archives; the -hp<password> token (header encryption with an inline password) is rarely used by legitimate users and is the actor's recurring staging signature. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admins archiving log bundles or backups with a password for transport
  • Legitimate use of WinRAR with -hp by a power user securing personal data
  • Backup software that wraps RAR with header encryption
  • Developers packaging release artifacts with a protected archive
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Backup\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the archive path and contents source — large archives built from web roots, database export folders, or user document trees signal staging. Check which process invoked rar (web shell = high severity). 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the archive, and watch for immediate outbound transfer to the actor IPs. 3) Hunt: correlate the archive creation time with subsequent curl/POST egress and SoftEther tunnel activity; sweep peer hosts for the same -hp pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-hp\S+"
| where ProcessCommandLine has " a "
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-hp\S+"
| where CommandLine has " a "
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Beyond IOCs: AI-enabled threat intelligence
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "853baab97b1f3b03c1ffa55797e87867f5fb7ce33457411f56afd270cb395453", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "41acb30b9d662d48b7b4fc0ac3d4b79f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Prototype-pollution payload (__proto__/constructor.prototype) in HTTP request to i18next missing-key route AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound web requests carrying prototype-pollution key tokens ("__proto__", "constructor.prototype") that abuse i18next-fs-backend ≤2.6.5's missing-key persistence (CVE-2026-48713) to walk into Object.prototype. Article-specific because it keys on the exact dotted-segment strings the setPath/getLastOfPath walker fails to guard, delivered via untrusted request bodies to a saveMissing route. Rationale: Uses the exact unsafe segments the article names as unguarded in getLastOfPath ("__proto__", "constructor", "prototype") split on the default "." keySeparator; "__proto__" and "constructor.prototype" in a request URI are extremely rare in benign traffic, so this is high-fidelity for the delivery of the pollution payload. i18next-http-middleware dotted prototype-pollution key in HTTP request (CVE-2026-48714) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound web requests carrying a translation key whose segment is a reserved name followed by the keySeparator (e.g. '__proto__.polluted', 'constructor.prototype.x') — the exact dotted bypass of the <=3.9.6 literal denylist that i18next-http-middleware's missingKeyHandler passes to i18next-fs-backend's unguarded setPath(). Article-specific: the '(__proto__|constructor|prototype).' segment shape is the CVE-2026-48714 payload signature, not a generic prototype-pollution template. Rationale: Uses the article's exact bypass string — a reserved segment (__proto__/constructor/prototype) followed by the default '.' keySeparator — which the 3.9.3 literal denylist misses. Legit i18next keys ('header.title') never start a segment with these names, so the '(reserved).' regex is high-fidelity; %2e branch catches URL-encoded delivery. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f49m-vf83-692w • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48714 • https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-middleware/commit/7c6d26f137d3e940b8d229ca148bca38845faf49
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal DAST/vuln scanner (Burp, Nessus, ZAP) fuzzing the app with __proto__ payloads
  • Security research / red-team validation traffic against a staging host
  • A backend that legitimately uses a dotted key literally containing the word 'constructor' as free text (rare)
  • WAF that reflects the offending payload into its own alert Message field, double-counting the same request
Suppression filter
| where RequestURL has "/locales/add/" or Message has "/locales/add/" or RequestContext has "/locales/add/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request from the WAF/proxy log — confirm the payload targets '/locales/add/<lng>/<ns>' and that the segment is a reserved name + '.', then check whether the request returned 2xx (delivered) vs blocked. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF and, if missingKeyHandler is exposed unauthenticated, disable the route or set saveMissing:false immediately; verify the app runs i18next-http-middleware >=3.9.7 and i18next-fs-backend >=2.6.6. 3) Hunt: search for the same source IP hitting other endpoints, look for post-request app crashes/500s or anomalous auth-bypass behaviour indicating successful Object.prototype pollution, and review whether persisted locale files were modified.

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step Gamaredon adopted from 2025-09-26: a malicious RAR archive exploiting WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 (alternate-data-stream path traversal) to write an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK downloader into the user's Startup folder so it auto-runs at next login. Article-specific because it pins the writing process to WinRAR-family binaries and the target to the Startup directory. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete persistence pivot (CVE-2025-8088 → HTA/VBS into Startup folder, active from 2025-09-26) and the WinRAR extraction binaries; Mandiant/Google and SOC Prime confirm the same ADS-to-Startup write pattern (.hta/.vbs/.vbe) across multiple Russia-aligned actors, so it is second-sourced. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability • https://socprime.com/active-threats/cve-2025-8088-critical-winrar-vulnerability/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/winrar-path-traversal-flaw-still-exploited-by-numerous-hackers/amp/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Software that bundles an updater shortcut into Startup after archive extraction
  • Security/portable apps extracted with WinRAR that create a startup auto-run by design

| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/sfx","setup","install") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the dropped file's full path/hash and the parent RAR archive; detonate or read the HTA/VBS content for a download URL and confirm WinRAR version < 7.13 on the host. 2) Contain: delete/quarantine the Startup-folder artifact, isolate the host before next logon (the payload fires at login), and block any URLs/domains found in the script. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same archive SHA256 in mail/download telemetry, for other hosts running unpatched WinRAR, and for follow-on mshta/wscript execution and connections to telegra.ph / gofile.io / S3 storage domains.

| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("hta","vbs","vbe","lnk")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
